draft.title: Compound interest by repeated percentages
card: With compound interest, each period's interest is added to the balance. The next period then earns interest on the new, larger balance, so it earns interest on interest.
To add a rate of \(5\%\) to an amount, multiply by \(1.05\). The multiplier is 1 plus the rate as a decimal.
Multiply by the multiplier once for each period. After 3 periods you multiply by it 3 times.
$1000 earns \(10\%\) each year, compounded. After year 1: \(1000 \times 1.1 = 1100\). After year 2: \(1100 \times 1.1 = 1210\). The year 2 interest is $110, not $100.
draft.remember: Compound interest: multiply by 1 plus the rate, once for each period.

a.q: Which multiplier adds \(8\%\) compound interest for one period?
a.why: Adding \(8\%\) means keeping the whole amount and adding \(0.08\) of it, so you multiply by \(1.08\). Multiplying by \(0.08\) would find only the interest, not the new balance.
a.clue: Keep the whole amount, then add the rate as a decimal.

b.q: Ava invests $2000 at \(10\%\) per year, compounded yearly. What is the balance after 2 years?
b.why: Year 1: \(2000 \times 1.1 = 2200\). Year 2: \(2200 \times 1.1 = 2420\). The tempting $2400 adds $200 each year, but year 2 interest is earned on $2200, so it is $220.
b.clue: Year 2 interest is worked out on the new balance.
